title: Reactions, Ethanol, Ethanoic Acid and Soaps

items.title: Today's lesson
items.content:
A **sooty pot** on a gas stove and **soap that will not lather** in borewell water open the lesson.

Four kinds of reactions follow: **combustion, oxidation, addition and substitution**. Then two important compounds, **ethanol** and **ethanoic acid**, and their reactions, including making **esters**.

The lesson ends with **how soaps and detergents clean**, and why soap fails in hard water.

items.title: You already know
items.content:
• saturated (single bonds) and unsaturated (double or triple bonds) hydrocarbons

• functional groups: alcohol —OH, carboxylic acid —COOH

• acids turn blue litmus red and react with carbonates to give CO₂

items.title: By the end, you can
items.content:
**1.** Describe combustion, oxidation, addition and substitution reactions.

**2.** Describe the properties and reactions of ethanol.

**3.** Describe the properties and reactions of ethanoic acid, including esterification.

**4.** Explain how soaps and detergents clean.

chunks.name: A black pot and a bucket of scum

items.text:
**What this shows**

Left: a pot on a gas stove. The flame is **yellow and smoky**, and the base of the pot has turned **black**.

**Answer to Question 1**

Take guesses and leave it open. Too little air reaches the flame, so the gas does not burn completely; the black layer is unburnt **carbon (soot)** (Part 1).

**What this shows**

Right: the same borewell water in two buckets. **Soap** in the left one gives a white scum; **detergent** in the right one gives plenty of foam.

**Answer to Question 2**

Take guesses and leave it open. Borewell water is often **hard**; soap reacts with the salts in it (Part 5).

**Step 1: start here**

Read the key idea: burning in oxygen gives **CO₂, water, heat and light**. Then go to the two flames (pointer 2).

**What this shows**

**Step 2.** A metal plate held over two flames: (a) the gas of a laboratory burner; (b) burning naphthalene.

**Answer to Question 3**

**Step 3.** (a) The burner gives a **clean blue flame** and the plate stays clean. (b) Naphthalene gives a **yellow, smoky flame**; the black layer is **soot**, unburnt carbon.

**Step 4**

Read the key idea: **blue flame** for saturated fuels, **sooty flame** for unsaturated ones or too little air. Question 1 from the hook is now answered.

items.text:
**Step 1: start here**

Read the key idea: combustion is **fast** oxidation; ethanol can also be oxidised **slowly**. Then go to the experiment (pointer 2).

**What this shows**

**Step 2.** Alkaline potassium permanganate is added drop by drop to warm ethanol: (a) the first few drops; (b) after many more drops.

**Answer to Question 4**

**Step 3.** The permanganate is **used up** as it adds oxygen to ethanol, so its colour disappears. Once **all the ethanol has been oxidised**, extra permanganate is not used up, so the purple stays.

items.prompt: Which is the balanced equation for the complete combustion of ethane, $\mathrm{C_{2}H_{6}}$, and what kind of flame would you expect?

items.text:
**On this question**

**A**: 4 C and 12 H on the right need 2 $\mathrm{C_{2}H_{6}}$; 8 O in CO₂ + 6 O in water = 14 O, so **7** $\mathrm{O_{2}}$. Ethane is **saturated**, so with enough air it burns with a clean blue flame. (B) is not balanced: 7 O on the right, 6 on the left.

script.x: Activate the question and explain depending on time available.

items.text:
**Answer to Question 5**

**Ethane**, $\mathrm{C_{2}H_{6}}$: one bond of the double bond opens, and a hydrogen atom joins **each carbon**. Let students try it before revealing the figure.

**What this shows**

Hydrogen **adds** across the double bond of ethene, with a **nickel catalyst**: ethene (unsaturated) becomes ethane (saturated). The circled atoms are the added hydrogens.

script.x: Question 5 first, before showing the figure. Answer is on pointer 1.
Then reveal the figure. Pointer 2 sets it up.
Show the key idea: addition, catalysts and hydrogenation. Its last line leads into the next slide.

items.text:
**Step 1: a substitution reaction**

Methane and chlorine **in sunlight**. Say the name aloud: this is a **substitution reaction**. The H of methane (orange) and one Cl (green) face each other and **leave together as HCl**; the other Cl takes the H's place on the carbon: chloromethane.

**Answer to Question 6**

**Step 2.** Nothing is added across a bond. A chlorine atom **replaces** a hydrogen atom: a **substitution reaction**. With more chlorine, more hydrogens are replaced, giving $\mathrm{CH_{2}Cl_{2}}$, $\mathrm{CHCl_{3}}$ and $\mathrm{CCl_{4}}$.

script.x: Show the reaction. Pointer 1 names it: a substitution reaction.

items.prompt:
Name the type of each reaction.
(i) $\mathrm{CH_{4} + 2O_{2}  \longrightarrow  CO_{2} + 2H_{2}O}$
(ii) $\mathrm{CH_{4} + Cl_{2}  \longrightarrow  CH_{3}Cl + HCl}$ in sunlight
(iii) $\mathrm{CH_{3}CH_{2}OH  \longrightarrow  CH_{3}COOH}$ with alkaline $\mathrm{KMnO_{4}}$
(iv) $\mathrm{C_{2}H_{4} + H_{2}  \longrightarrow  C_{2}H_{6}}$ with nickel

items.text:
**On this question**

**C**: (i) burning in oxygen: **combustion**. (ii) Cl replaces H: **substitution**. (iii) an oxidising agent turns ethanol into ethanoic acid: **oxidation**. (iv) H₂ adds across C=C: **addition**.

script.x: Activate the question and explain depending on time available.

items.text:
**Step 1: start here**

Read the key idea: ethanol's properties and uses, and why industrial ethanol is **denatured**. Then go to the experiment (pointer 2).

**What this shows**

**Step 2.** A small piece of **sodium** dropped into ethanol: gas bubbles form; a burning match is brought to the mouth of the tube.

**Answer to Question 7**

**Step 3. Hydrogen.** $\mathrm{2Na}$ + $\mathrm{2CH_{3}CH_{2}OH}$ $\longrightarrow$ $\mathrm{2CH_{3}CH_{2}O^{-}Na^{+}}$ + $\mathrm{H_{2}}$; the other product is **sodium ethoxide**.

**Step 1: start here**

Read the key idea: hot concentrated sulphuric acid removes **water** from ethanol. Then show the figure (pointer 2).

**What this shows**

**Step 2.** The circled H and OH leave ethanol as **water**, and a **double bond** forms between the two carbons: ethene.

script.x: Show the conclusion box, pointing back to the dehydration figure.

items.prompt: Compound X, $\mathrm{C_{2}H_{6}O}$, is heated with excess concentrated sulphuric acid at 443 K to give Y. Y reacts with hydrogen in the presence of nickel to give Z. Identify X, Y and Z.
options: X ethanol, Y ethane, Z ethene
X ethanol, Y ethene, Z ethane
X ethanoic acid, Y ethene, Z ethane
X ethene, Y ethanol, Z ethane

items.text:
**On this question**

**B**: X is **ethanol**. Hot concentrated sulphuric acid removes water (**dehydration**), giving **ethene** (Y). Hydrogen adds across its double bond (**addition**), giving **ethane** (Z).

script.x: Activate the question and explain depending on time available.

items.text:
**Step 1: start here**

Read the key idea: **vinegar** and **glacial acetic acid**. Then ask Question 8 (pointer 2).

**Answer to Question 8**

**Step 2. Hydrochloric acid** shows the lower pH. It is a **strong acid**, fully ionised in water; ethanoic acid is a **weak acid** and only partly ionised, so it gives fewer hydrogen ions. Then reveal the figure (pointer 3).

**Step 3: reveal after Question 8**

The universal-indicator result: hydrochloric acid turns it **red** (pH ≈ 1), ethanoic acid **orange** (pH ≈ 3 to 4). Keep it hidden until students have predicted.

script.x: Pointer 3: reveal the indicator result to confirm.

items.text:
**Step 1: start here**

Read the key idea: even as a weak acid, ethanoic acid reacts with **bases** and **carbonates** like other acids. It also reacts with **alcohols**: go to the experiment (pointer 2).

**What this shows**

**Step 2.** (a) Ethanol, ethanoic acid and a few drops of **concentrated sulphuric acid** are warmed in a water bath. (b) The mixture is poured into water and **smelled**.

**Answer to Question 9**

**Step 3.** A **new substance** has formed: an **ester**. Esters have sweet, fruity smells.

**What this shows**

**Step 4.** The acid's OH and the alcohol's H (circled) leave as **water**; the rest join to form **ethyl ethanoate**, an ester.

script.x: Pointer 1: show the key idea on reactions with bases and carbonates.

**Step 1: start here**

Read the key idea with the ester equation above as a reminder: **esterification**, and its reverse with NaOH, **saponification**. Then show the conclusion.

items.prompt: Two unlabelled bottles hold ethanol and ethanoic acid. A pinch of sodium hydrogencarbonate is added to a little of each. What is seen?
options: Both give brisk bubbles of hydrogen
Ethanol gives brisk bubbles of CO₂; ethanoic acid shows no change
Ethanoic acid gives brisk bubbles of CO₂; ethanol shows no change

items.text:
**On this question**

**C**: ethanoic acid is an acid, so it reacts with a hydrogencarbonate: $\mathrm{CH_{3}COOH}$ + $\mathrm{NaHCO_{3}}$ $\longrightarrow$ $\mathrm{CH_{3}COONa}$ + $\mathrm{H_{2}O}$ + $\mathrm{CO_{2}}$. Ethanol is not an acid, so nothing happens. The gas turns lime water milky.

items.text:
**Step 1: start here**

Read the key idea: what a soap is. Then show one soap molecule (pointer 2).

**What this shows**

**Step 2.** One soap molecule: a **long hydrocarbon tail** (like a hydrocarbon, it mixes with oil, not water) and an **ionic head** (charged, so it mixes with water).

**Answer to Question 10**

**Step 3.** The **tails** go into the oil; the **ionic heads** stay in the water, so the molecules gather round the drop. Next slide shows the result.

script.x: Pointer 3: Question 10. Students sketch their guess before the next slide.

items.text:
**What this shows**

**Step 1.** Soap molecules round a drop of oily dirt: **tails in the oil, heads in the water**. Compare it with the students' sketches from Question 10.

**Step 2**

Read the key idea: the cluster is a **micelle**, and rinsing carries it away.

items.text:
**What this shows**

**Step 1.** Equal amounts of soap or detergent shaken with (a) distilled water, (b) hard water, (c) hard water.

**Answer to Question 11**

**Step 2.** Hard water contains **calcium and magnesium salts**. Soap reacts with them to form an **insoluble** substance, **scum**, so much of the soap is wasted and little foam forms. Question 2 from the hook is now answered.

**Step 3**

Why does (c), the detergent, still foam? Read the key idea.

items.prompt: Soap is added to water containing a drop of oil. Which figure shows how the soap molecules arrange themselves round the oil? (circle: ionic head; zigzag: hydrocarbon tail)

items.text:
**On this question**

**B**: the **tails point into the oil** and the **ionic heads face the water**: a micelle. (A) has the tails sticking out into the water; (C) shows no micelle; (D) mixes heads and tails.
